Unit Distance Points

CoordinatesGraph TheoryUnit Distance Problem
Game: Place a few points so that as many pairs of them as possible are exactly one step apart. Beat the target for each number of points.
How to play: Drag the dots. A pair that is exactly one step apart (the length of the little ruler) gets a line. Dots stick to the right distance when you get close. With the keyboard, press Space to pick the next dot and the arrow keys to move it.

Look for the math

Draw n points in the plane and join every pair that is exactly 1 apart. How many lines can you get? This is the unit distance problem that Paul Erdős posed in 1946.

Triangles are the building block

Two points can have one line, three can have three (an equilateral triangle), and four can have five (two triangles glued along an edge, a rhombus). Pieces of the triangular lattice give the best arrangements for 3 to 8 points: 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 14. The page checks that a lattice cannot beat these for up to 6 points.

Nine points need a twist

The triangular lattice gives only 17 lines for 9 points, but 18 is possible. Take an equilateral triangle, and a copy turned by a small angle. Add every point of the first to every point of the second. The 9 sums have 4 neighbours each, so 9 × 4 / 2 = 18 lines. The test builds this arrangement and counts it.

The question for many points

Write u(n) for the most unit pairs among n points. Exact values are known only for small n, so the real question is how u(n) grows. The next pages show Erdős's grid construction, which beats n by a hair, and the argument that it cannot beat n4/3. Both are far apart, and no one knew which was closer to the truth until the 2026 disproof of Erdős's conjecture.

Try 5 points first: can you get 7 lines? Then see what the 6-point answer adds to it.

An original game for coolmaths, after a problem posed by Paul Erdős in 1946 (Wikipedia)
